one_paragraph_summary: Panganiban says VP Sara Duterte's impeachment has revived a constitutional numbers game, but the real turning point is the pretrial concluded on June 25, before the trial proper begins on July 6. The Constitution requires two-thirds of all Senate members to convict -- academically 16 of 24. He shares two retirees' views: SAJ Antonio T. Carpio counts only senators legally able to act, so preventively suspended Sen. Jinggoy Estrada is excluded under Trillanes v. Pimentel, while Sen. Dela Rosa, hiding from an ICC warrant, is not yet excluded because he has not been arrested; retired Justice Adolfo S. Azcuna argues that if Dela Rosa is judicially declared a fugitive and disentitled to his seat, that would amount to 'constructive resignation.' With due respect, CJP says the threshold matters only after the votes are cast: if 16 or more vote to convict, the debate is academic; only below 16 does the denominator become crucial. What matters now is the pretrial -- 'an essential device for the speedy disposition of disputes,' as his ponencia in Tiu v. Middleton put it -- where both sides lay their cards on the table. Impeachment is sui generis: no amicable settlement or plea bargaining; a possible resignation by VP Sara deserves its own column. Senate President Sherwin Gatchalian's June 9 notice sought stipulations, marking of evidence and witness lists (including 'Mary Grace Piattos'). The fuss over marking the 'BIR Green Box' was unwarranted, since marking is clerical; admissibility and weight are for the Impeachment Court. Senate Secretary Renato Bantug estimated 92 trial days, at least seven months. A nation's strength lies in the integrity of institutions ready to correct the frailties of those in power, and both sides must lay the procedural foundations to end the saga.
